passages.title: Air Pollution, Article 21 and the Delhi-NCR Framework
passages.passage: The right to a pollution-free environment is part of the right to life under Article 21. In Subhash Kumar v. State of Bihar (1991), the Supreme Court held that the right to life includes the right to enjoyment of pollution-free water and air for the full enjoyment of life. The Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981 provides for the prevention, control and abatement of air pollution, and for the declaration of air pollution control areas under Section 19; the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 empowers the Central Government under Section 3 to take all measures necessary for protecting and improving the environment. Delhi's air pollution has been supervised by the Supreme Court in the long-running M.C. Mehta v. Union of India litigation, in the course of which the Court directed in 1998 that the public transport fleet in Delhi be converted to compressed natural gas, and in Arjun Gopal v. Union of India (2017 and 2018) it first suspended the sale of firecrackers in Delhi-NCR and later permitted only 'green' crackers, limiting the hours of bursting. The Environment Pollution (Prevention and Control) Authority (EPCA), which the Court had constituted under the Environment (Protection) Act, was in 2021 replaced by the Commission for Air Quality Management in National Capital Region and Adjoining Areas, constituted under the Commission for Air Quality Management in National Capital Region and Adjoining Areas Act, 2021, which was passed after an Ordinance of October 2020. The Commission is a statutory body with the power to issue directions, to coordinate action among Delhi, Haryana, Punjab, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh, to restrict industries, and to address matters such as stubble burning, and its directions are binding, with penal consequences for non-compliance; it supersedes the powers of the State pollution control boards in the region, and an appeal from its orders lies to the Supreme Court. The Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP), implemented by the Commission, prescribes measures in four stages, linked to the Air Quality Index (AQI), from Stage I for 'poor' air quality (AQI 201-300) to Stage IV for 'severe plus' (AQI above 450), which include restrictions on construction, entry of trucks, and, in the severe stages, closure of schools and restrictions on vehicles. In dealing with pollution, the courts have relied on the 'polluter pays' principle, which makes the polluter liable for the cost of restoration and for compensation, the 'precautionary principle', under which lack of scientific certainty is not a ground for postponing measures to prevent degradation, and the 'public trust doctrine'. The Court has also urged States to provide support to farmers, such as machinery, to end stubble burning, while holding that the right to livelihood of persons engaged in polluting activities cannot override the right of the public to clean air.

passages.title: Standard Essential Patents, FRAND and the Delhi High Court
passages.passage: A standard essential patent (SEP) is a patent which claims an invention that must necessarily be used to comply with a technical standard, such as 3G, 4G or Wi-Fi, set by a standard-setting organisation. Since manufacturers cannot make a compliant device without using the patented technology, the owner of a SEP enjoys substantial market power. To balance this, patent holders commit, when the standard is adopted, to license on fair, reasonable and non-discriminatory (FRAND) terms. The potential for 'hold-up', in which a SEP holder demands excessive royalties under the threat of an injunction, and for 'hold-out', in which an implementer uses the technology but delays or refuses to pay or negotiate, are the two concerns which the law of SEPs seeks to address. The Patents Act, 1970 grants the patentee the exclusive right to prevent third parties from making, using, offering for sale, selling or importing the patented product (Section 48), and remedies for infringement include an injunction, damages or an account of profits (Section 108). The Act does not contain any special provision on SEPs, which have been developed through judicial decisions, mostly of the Delhi High Court, which has been the principal forum for these disputes. In Telefonaktiebolaget LM Ericsson v. Lava International Ltd. (2024), the Delhi High Court awarded the patentee damages of about Rs 244 crore, which is regarded as the first major decision in India to award damages for infringement of SEPs; the Court found that the defendant was an 'unwilling licensee', which had used the technology without taking a licence or paying royalties, and held that an implementer who is unwilling to negotiate cannot claim the benefit of the FRAND commitment. The Delhi High Court has, in several cases, ordered implementers to deposit sums as 'pro tem security', pending the determination of the royalty, in order to prevent hold-out. Concerns about hold-up, on the other side, have been raised under competition law, since Section 4 of the Competition Act, 2002 prohibits abuse of a dominant position, including the imposition of unfair prices, and the Competition Commission has examined complaints against SEP holders. The relationship between the Patents Act and the Competition Act has been contested before the High Court, in view of Section 60 of the Competition Act, under which its provisions have effect notwithstanding anything inconsistent in any other law, and of Section 62, under which its provisions are in addition to and not in derogation of other laws. Section 84 of the Patents Act also permits a compulsory licence where the reasonable requirements of the public have not been satisfied or the invention is not available at a reasonably affordable price.
